---
title: "How do you reshape data so a model can use it?"
subtitle: "Turn correlated predictors until they stop repeating each other, bend a lopsided response until its spread is even, and take out a shared trend before it passes for a relationship."
engine: knitr
---

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="pca-figure" data-step="0" data-caption="Fig. 1 · two predictors that mostly repeat each other · made-up data, centred, same units"}
:::

You are building a regression model and you have 50 predictors. Many of them measure nearly the same thing, the way an assessment score and a homework score do. That overlap causes three problems at once. Correlated predictors make the coefficients unstable, which is **multicollinearity**. Many predictors relative to the number of data points invite overfitting. And some of the predictors are mostly noise.

If two features carry almost the same information, you do not need both. Look at the figure: neither axis runs along the cloud. The points spread along a diagonal, and each axis only sees part of that spread. Principal component analysis, PCA, finds the directions the data really varies along and lets you keep only those.

## Turning the axes

Draw a line through the centre of the cloud and drop every point straight onto it. Those landing spots are the **projections**, and their variance tells you how much of the spread that line captures. Turn the line and the number changes.

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="pca-figure" data-step="1" data-caption="Fig. 2 · turn the line and watch the variance of the projections · computed live · made-up data"}
:::

One angle gives the largest variance. That direction is the first principal component, **PC1**. The second, **PC2**, is perpendicular to it and takes the most of whatever spread is left, and so on for as many dimensions as you have. PCA is a rotation of the coordinate system: nothing is stretched and no point moves relative to the others. In the rotated space the components are uncorrelated with each other, which is what removes the multicollinearity.

You do not have to search by turning a line. The recipe is: standardise the data so each feature has mean 0 and standard deviation 1, compute the covariance matrix ($\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X}$), find its eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and sort them by eigenvalue, largest first. The first eigenvector is PC1, the second is PC2.

| Concept | What it is | Plain English |
|:--------|:-----------|:-------------|
| **Eigenvector** | A direction in feature space | Which way does the data spread? |
| **Eigenvalue** | A number paired with each eigenvector | How much variance is in that direction? |

## What an eigenvalue describes

The eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue points in the direction of maximum variance. In the curve beside Fig. 2, the top of the hill is the first eigenvalue and the bottom of the valley is the second. Divide an eigenvalue by the sum of all of them and you have the share of the total variance that component carries.

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="pca-figure" data-step="2" data-steps="2:both components|3:keep only PC1" data-caption="Fig. 3 · the components from the covariance matrix, then the cloud reduced to one of them · made-up data"}
:::

Now read the two lines of arithmetic beside the figure. PC1 is some amount of $x_1$ plus some amount of $x_2$. So is PC2. Neither component is one of your original variables; each is a blend of all of them. The eigenvalue is the variance along that blend. [Exam trap: eigenvalues describe the components, not the original covariates. PCA rotates the space, and every component mixes all the original variables. A large first eigenvalue tells you PC1 matters. It does not tell you that $x_1$, or any single covariate, matters.]{.side}

With correlated data, PC1 often carries so much that you can drop PC2 and lose very little. Press "keep only PC1" and each point slides onto the line: two numbers per point become one, and the variance you gave up is exactly the second eigenvalue. Two features are easy to draw, but the method earns its keep when it compresses many features into a few components. In the R below, ten correlated features driven by two hidden factors need only a handful of components to hold 90% of the variance. The rest is mostly noise.

To choose how many to keep, plot the eigenvalues (or the percent of variance) for each component. This is the **scree plot**, and it is read like the elbow plot for k-means: look for the place where the curve flattens and keep the components before the drop-off. The alternative rule is to keep components until the cumulative variance explained reaches 80 to 90%.

## What PCA cannot see

PCA ranks components by variance in X. It never looks at the response, so it does not rank them by predictive power for Y. A high-variance component might be irrelevant noise, and a low-variance component might hold the signal you need. The R below builds exactly that case: PC1 has the most variance and the least correlation with the response, and PC3 has the least variance and the most. [Exam trap: "keep the components with the most variance" and "keep the components that predict best" are different rules. Do not drop low-variance components blindly.]{.side}

So treat PCA as a preprocessing step. The usual workflow is: start with many correlated predictors, run PCA to get uncorrelated components, use cross-validation to decide how many to keep, feed those components into regression (or SVM, KNN and so on), and validate the final model on test data. In the ten-feature example, three components reach a similar adjusted $R^2$ to all ten predictors, with a simpler model, less overfitting risk and no multicollinearity.

Three things have to hold before PCA is worth running. Scaling is the one that bites: with income in the tens of thousands and age in the tens, unscaled PCA simply reports that income has bigger numbers.

| Requirement | Why | What happens if violated |
|:------------|:----|:------------------------|
| **Standardize first** | Features with larger ranges dominate | PCA reflects scale, not importance |
| **Continuous features** | PCA assumes linear relationships | Binary/categorical features need other methods |
| **Some correlation** | If features are uncorrelated, PCA can't compress | You get back the same features |

## Bending the response

A different problem needs a different fix. Regression assumes **constant variance**: the residuals should be spread about equally everywhere. Real data often breaks this. Plot the residuals against the fitted values and you see a funnel, tight on the left and wide on the right. That is **heteroscedasticity**, and it makes the model's predictions unreliable: accurate for small values, wildly off for large ones.

The Box-Cox transformation fixes it by transforming the response:

$$T(y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{y^{\lambda} - 1}{\lambda} & \text{if } \lambda \neq 0 \\[6pt] \log(y) & \text{if } \lambda = 0 \end{cases}$$

Here $y$ is the original response, the thing you are predicting, $T(y)$ is the stabilised version, and the power $\lambda$ controls the shape of the transformation. A few values of $\lambda$ are worth knowing by name. [At λ = 0 the top formula would divide by zero, so the log takes its place. The response has to be positive for any of this to work.]{.side}

| $\lambda$ | Transform | Effect |
|:---------:|:----------|:-------|
| 1 | $y$ (no change) | Data is fine as-is |
| 0.5 | $\sqrt{y}$ | Mild compression of large values |
| 0 | $\log(y)$ | Strong compression — common in practice |
| -1 | $1/y$ | Very aggressive compression |

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="boxcox-figure" data-step="0" data-caption="Fig. 4 · a lopsided sample at λ = 1, with the bell curve of the same mean and spread · made-up data"}
:::

You do not pick $\lambda$ by eye. Box-Cox finds the best value automatically by trying different values and taking the one that makes the residuals most normally distributed. Fig. 4 shows the starting point on a single lopsided sample: at $\lambda = 1$ the large values trail off in a long tail and a bell curve does not fit.

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="boxcox-figure" data-step="1" data-steps="1:the log|2:slide λ" data-caption="Fig. 5 · the same sample, transformed live in your browser · made-up data"}
:::

As $\lambda$ falls, the large values are pulled in harder and the tail shortens. Slide it and watch the skewness: somewhere near the log it crosses zero, and if you keep going the transform overshoots. Applied to a real response, the right $\lambda$ makes the funnel in the residual plot disappear and leaves residuals that are more uniform and more normal.

## Taking out the trend

Sometimes the trouble is time. When you want to study the relationship between X and Y but both are trending over time, the shared trend creates a **spurious correlation**. Ice cream sales and drownings both climb through the months of the example below, and they correlate strongly without one having anything to do with the other.

The fix is to remove the trend first and analyse what is left. Fit a line against time and subtract it:

$$y_{\text{detrended}} = y - (\hat{a}_0 + \hat{a}_1 \cdot \text{time})$$

Do this to both variables and compare the detrended versions. Once the time trend is gone, the spurious correlation goes with it.

## Run it yourself {.reference}

Every plot below is produced by the R on this page. Open "The R" under any of them to see the code.

Two features that carry overlapping information.

```{r}
#| label: plot-correlated-data
#| fig-cap: "These two features are highly correlated — they carry redundant information"

library(ggplot2)
set.seed(42)

n <- 100

# Two correlated features
x1 <- rnorm(n, 50, 10)
x2 <- 0.8 * x1 + rnorm(n, 10, 5)  # correlated with x1

df <- data.frame(x1 = x1, x2 = x2)

ggplot(df, aes(x1, x2)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, color = "gray40") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(x = "Feature 1 (e.g., assessment score)",
       y = "Feature 2 (e.g., homework score)",
       title = paste0("Correlation = ", round(cor(x1, x2), 2),
                       " — these carry overlapping information"))
```

The same data standardised, with the PCA directions drawn on it, and then in the rotated space. PC1 (horizontal) holds the main spread, PC2 (vertical) holds what is left, and the two are uncorrelated.

```{r}
#| label: plot-pca-rotation
#| fig-cap: "PCA rotates the axes to align with the directions of maximum variance"

# Standardize
df_s <- scale(df)

# PCA
pca <- prcomp(df_s)

# Plot original data with PCA directions
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

# Original space with PCA arrows
plot(df_s[, 1], df_s[, 2], pch = 19, col = "gray40", asp = 1,
  main = "Original Space + PCA Directions",
  xlab = "Feature 1 (standardized)", ylab = "Feature 2 (standardized)")

# PC1 direction
arrows(0, 0, pca$rotation[1, 1] * 2, pca$rotation[2, 1] * 2,
  col = "coral", lwd = 3, length = 0.15)
text(pca$rotation[1, 1] * 2.3, pca$rotation[2, 1] * 2.3,
  "PC1", col = "coral", font = 2, cex = 1.2)

# PC2 direction
arrows(0, 0, pca$rotation[1, 2] * 1.5, pca$rotation[2, 2] * 1.5,
  col = "steelblue", lwd = 3, length = 0.15)
text(pca$rotation[1, 2] * 1.8, pca$rotation[2, 2] * 1.8,
  "PC2", col = "steelblue", font = 2, cex = 1.2)

# Rotated space (PCA scores)
scores <- pca$x
plot(scores[, 1], scores[, 2], pch = 19, col = "gray40", asp = 1,
  main = "PCA Space (Rotated)",
  xlab = "PC1 (most variance)", ylab = "PC2 (remaining variance)")
abline(h = 0, v = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray70")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The eigenvalues and the share of variance each component captures.

```{r}
#| label: plot-eigenvalues
#| fig-cap: "Eigenvalues tell you how much variance each component captures"

# Show eigenvalues
eigenvalues <- pca$sdev^2
var_explained <- eigenvalues / sum(eigenvalues) * 100

cat("Eigenvalues:\n")
cat(sprintf("  PC1: %.2f (%.1f%% of variance)\n", eigenvalues[1], var_explained[1]))
cat(sprintf("  PC2: %.2f (%.1f%% of variance)\n", eigenvalues[2], var_explained[2]))
cat(sprintf("\nPC1 alone captures %.1f%% of the information!\n", var_explained[1]))
cat("With correlated data, you can often drop PC2 and lose very little.")
```

Ten correlated features, all driven by two hidden factors, and how the variance piles up in the first few components.

```{r}
#| label: plot-high-dim
#| fig-cap: "10 correlated features compressed into components — most variance in first 2-3"

set.seed(42)

# Generate 10 correlated features (all driven by 2 hidden factors)
hidden1 <- rnorm(n)
hidden2 <- rnorm(n)

features <- matrix(nrow = n, ncol = 10)
for (j in 1:10) {
  w1 <- runif(1, 0.5, 1.5) * sample(c(-1, 1), 1)
  w2 <- runif(1, 0.2, 0.8) * sample(c(-1, 1), 1)
  features[, j] <- w1 * hidden1 + w2 * hidden2 + rnorm(n, 0, 0.5)
}
colnames(features) <- paste0("X", 1:10)

# PCA
pca10 <- prcomp(scale(features))
var_exp10 <- pca10$sdev^2 / sum(pca10$sdev^2) * 100
cum_var <- cumsum(var_exp10)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

# Scree plot
barplot(var_exp10, names.arg = paste0("PC", 1:10),
  col = ifelse(cum_var <= 90, "steelblue", "gray80"),
  main = "Scree Plot: Variance per Component",
  ylab = "% Variance Explained", las = 2)

# Cumulative variance
plot(1:10, cum_var, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2,
  main = "Cumulative Variance Explained",
  xlab = "Number of Components", ylab = "% Total Variance",
  ylim = c(0, 100))
abline(h = 90, lty = 2, col = "coral")
text(7, 85, "90% threshold", col = "coral", cex = 0.9)

# Mark how many needed for 90%
n_for_90 <- which(cum_var >= 90)[1]
points(n_for_90, cum_var[n_for_90], pch = 19, cex = 2, col = "coral")
text(n_for_90 + 1, cum_var[n_for_90] - 5,
  paste0(n_for_90, " components\nfor 90%"), col = "coral", cex = 0.9)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

**10 features → `r n_for_90` components** that capture 90%+ of the information. The remaining components are mostly noise.

The scree plot for the same ten features. Look for the elbow.

```{r}
#| label: plot-scree-elbow
#| fig-cap: "The scree plot elbow suggests 2-3 components are sufficient"

plot(1:10, pca10$sdev^2, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2,
  main = "Scree Plot: Look for the Elbow",
  xlab = "Component Number", ylab = "Eigenvalue")

# Highlight the elbow
points(3, pca10$sdev[3]^2, pch = 1, cex = 3, col = "coral", lwd = 2)
text(4.5, pca10$sdev[3]^2, "Elbow here →\nkeep 2-3 components",
  col = "coral", cex = 0.9)
```

The trap: data built so that the signal sits in a low-variance direction.

```{r}
#| label: plot-pca-trap
#| fig-cap: "PC1 has the most variance but PC3 actually predicts the response"

set.seed(42)

# Create data where the signal is in a low-variance direction
n_trap <- 150
noise_big <- rnorm(n_trap, 0, 5)    # big variance, no signal
noise_med <- rnorm(n_trap, 0, 3)    # medium variance, no signal
signal <- rnorm(n_trap, 0, 1)       # small variance, IS the signal

X_trap <- cbind(
  noise_big + 0.1 * signal,
  noise_med + 0.05 * signal,
  0.5 * noise_big + 0.8 * signal    # signal mixed in
)

y_trap <- 3 * signal + rnorm(n_trap, 0, 0.5)  # y depends on the hidden signal

pca_trap <- prcomp(scale(X_trap))

# Correlation of each PC with y
pc_cor <- sapply(1:3, function(j) cor(pca_trap$x[, j], y_trap))

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

barplot(pca_trap$sdev^2, names.arg = paste0("PC", 1:3),
  col = "steelblue", main = "Variance (what PCA ranks by)",
  ylab = "Eigenvalue")

barplot(abs(pc_cor), names.arg = paste0("PC", 1:3),
  col = c("gray70", "gray70", "coral"),
  main = "Correlation with Y (what matters!)",
  ylab = "|Correlation with response|")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

cat("PC1 has the MOST variance but the LEAST predictive power.\n")
cat("PC3 has the LEAST variance but the MOST predictive power.\n")
cat("\nThis is why you MUST validate PCA-based models on actual prediction.\n")
cat("Don't blindly drop low-variance components!")
```

Why you standardise first. Without scaling, the feature with the larger range dominates PC1.

```{r}
#| label: plot-scaling-pca
#| fig-cap: "Without scaling, the high-range feature dominates PC1"

set.seed(42)

# Income: 30k-90k, Age: 20-65
data_unscaled <- data.frame(
  income = rnorm(80, 60000, 15000),
  age = rnorm(80, 40, 10)
)

pca_unscaled <- prcomp(data_unscaled, scale. = FALSE)
pca_scaled <- prcomp(data_unscaled, scale. = TRUE)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

# Loadings comparison
barplot(abs(pca_unscaled$rotation[, 1]), names.arg = c("Income", "Age"),
  col = c("coral", "steelblue"), main = "PC1 Loadings: UNSCALED",
  ylab = "Absolute Loading")
mtext("Income dominates (larger range)", side = 1, line = 2.5, cex = 0.8, col = "red")

barplot(abs(pca_scaled$rotation[, 1]), names.arg = c("Income", "Age"),
  col = c("coral", "steelblue"), main = "PC1 Loadings: SCALED",
  ylab = "Absolute Loading")
mtext("Both contribute fairly", side = 1, line = 2.5, cex = 0.8, col = "darkgreen")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Heteroscedasticity: the spread of the response grows with x, and the residual plot shows a funnel.

```{r}
#| label: plot-heteroscedasticity
#| fig-cap: "The funnel shape: variance increases with the predicted value"

set.seed(42)
x_bc <- runif(100, 1, 20)
y_bc <- 2 * x_bc + rnorm(100, 0, x_bc * 0.8)  # variance grows with x

df_bc <- data.frame(x = x_bc, y = y_bc)
fit_bc <- lm(y ~ x, data = df_bc)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

plot(df_bc$x, df_bc$y, pch = 19, col = "gray40",
  main = "Data: Variance Grows with X",
  xlab = "X", ylab = "Y")
abline(fit_bc, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)

plot(fitted(fit_bc), residuals(fit_bc), pch = 19, col = "gray40",
  main = "Residual Plot: Funnel Shape",
  xlab = "Fitted Values", ylab = "Residuals")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "coral")
text(25, 15, "Variance increases →\n(heteroscedasticity)", col = "coral", cex = 0.9)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The Box-Cox profile from `MASS::boxcox`, and the optimal $\lambda$ it finds.

```{r}
#| label: plot-boxcox-lambda
#| fig-cap: "Box-Cox finds the optimal λ that stabilizes variance"

library(MASS)

# Need positive y for Box-Cox
y_pos <- y_bc - min(y_bc) + 1
df_pos <- data.frame(x = x_bc, y = y_pos)
fit_pos <- lm(y ~ x, data = df_pos)

# Box-Cox profile
bc <- boxcox(fit_pos, plotit = TRUE)

# Find optimal lambda
optimal_lambda <- bc$x[which.max(bc$y)]
cat(sprintf("\nOptimal λ = %.2f\n", optimal_lambda))
cat(sprintf("Closest standard transform: %s\n",
  ifelse(abs(optimal_lambda) < 0.2, "log(y)",
    ifelse(abs(optimal_lambda - 0.5) < 0.2, "√y",
      ifelse(abs(optimal_lambda - 1) < 0.2, "no transform needed",
        paste0("y^", round(optimal_lambda, 2)))))))
```

Residuals before and after the transform.

```{r}
#| label: plot-boxcox-effect
#| fig-cap: "Before and after Box-Cox: the funnel shape disappears"

# Apply transform
if (abs(optimal_lambda) < 0.01) {
  y_transformed <- log(y_pos)
} else {
  y_transformed <- (y_pos^optimal_lambda - 1) / optimal_lambda
}

df_trans <- data.frame(x = x_bc, y = y_transformed)
fit_trans <- lm(y ~ x, data = df_trans)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

# Before
plot(fitted(fit_pos), residuals(fit_pos), pch = 19, col = "coral",
  main = "BEFORE Box-Cox: Residuals",
  xlab = "Fitted", ylab = "Residual")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)

hist(residuals(fit_pos), breaks = 15, col = "coral", border = "white",
  main = "BEFORE: Residual Distribution", xlab = "Residual")

# After
plot(fitted(fit_trans), residuals(fit_trans), pch = 19, col = "steelblue",
  main = "AFTER Box-Cox: Residuals",
  xlab = "Fitted", ylab = "Residual")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)

hist(residuals(fit_trans), breaks = 15, col = "steelblue", border = "white",
  main = "AFTER: Residual Distribution", xlab = "Residual")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Two unrelated series that both trend upward, before and after detrending.

```{r}
#| label: plot-detrending
#| fig-cap: "Both variables trend upward with time → spurious correlation. Detrending reveals the truth."

set.seed(42)
time_dt <- 1:60

# Two UNRELATED things that both trend upward
ice_cream <- 10 + 0.3 * time_dt + rnorm(60, 0, 2)
drownings <- 5 + 0.15 * time_dt + rnorm(60, 0, 1.5)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

# Raw correlation (spurious)
plot(ice_cream, drownings, pch = 19, col = "coral",
  main = paste0("Raw: r = ", round(cor(ice_cream, drownings), 2)),
  xlab = "Ice Cream Sales", ylab = "Drownings")
abline(lm(drownings ~ ice_cream), col = "coral", lwd = 2)

# Both trending
plot(time_dt, ice_cream, type = "l", col = "coral", lwd = 2,
  main = "Both variables trend with time",
  xlab = "Time", ylab = "Value", ylim = c(0, 35))
lines(time_dt, drownings, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
legend("topleft", legend = c("Ice cream", "Drownings"), bty = "n",
  col = c("coral", "steelblue"), lwd = 2, cex = 0.8)

# Detrend
ice_dt <- residuals(lm(ice_cream ~ time_dt))
drown_dt <- residuals(lm(drownings ~ time_dt))

# Detrended correlation (real)
plot(ice_dt, drown_dt, pch = 19, col = "steelblue",
  main = paste0("Detrended: r = ", round(cor(ice_dt, drown_dt), 2)),
  xlab = "Ice Cream (detrended)", ylab = "Drownings (detrended)")
abline(lm(drown_dt ~ ice_dt), col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)

# Detrended series
plot(time_dt, ice_dt, type = "l", col = "coral", lwd = 2,
  main = "After detrending: no trend",
  xlab = "Time", ylab = "Detrended Value")
lines(time_dt, drown_dt, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray50")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

PCA followed by regression: three components against all ten predictors.

```{r}
#| label: plot-pca-regression
#| fig-cap: "PCA + regression: compress 10 features into 3 components, then regress"

# Use the 10-feature data from earlier
y_demo <- 2 * hidden1 - 1.5 * hidden2 + rnorm(n, 0, 0.5)

# Full regression (all 10 features)
fit_full <- lm(y_demo ~ features)

# PCA regression (3 components)
scores3 <- pca10$x[, 1:3]
fit_pca <- lm(y_demo ~ scores3)

cat("=== Full model (10 predictors) ===\n")
cat(sprintf("  R² = %.3f\n", summary(fit_full)$r.squared))
cat(sprintf("  Adj R² = %.3f\n\n", summary(fit_full)$adj.r.squared))

cat("=== PCA model (3 components) ===\n")
cat(sprintf("  R² = %.3f\n", summary(fit_pca)$r.squared))
cat(sprintf("  Adj R² = %.3f\n", summary(fit_pca)$adj.r.squared))
cat("\n10 predictors → 3 components with similar Adj R²")
cat("\nSimpler model, less overfitting risk, no multicollinearity")
```

## On one page {.reference}

```
PCA RECIPE
==========

1. PURPOSE: Compress many correlated features into fewer uncorrelated components

2. ALGORITHM:
   Standardize → Covariance matrix → Eigenvalues/vectors → Sort by variance

3. KEY CONCEPTS:
   Eigenvector = direction of spread (becomes a component)
   Eigenvalue = how much variance in that direction
   PC1 = most variance, PC2 = second most, etc.

4. HOW MANY COMPONENTS?
   Scree plot elbow OR cumulative variance ≥ 80-90%

5. CRITICAL TRAP:
   PCA ranks by VARIANCE in X, not by PREDICTIVE POWER for Y
   High-variance PC might be noise. Low-variance PC might be the signal.
   ALWAYS validate with cross-validation.

6. REQUIREMENTS:
   - ALWAYS standardize first (scale. = TRUE)
   - Continuous features
   - Some correlation among features (otherwise PCA can't compress)

7. EIGENVALUES DESCRIBE COMPONENTS, NOT ORIGINAL VARIABLES:
   PCA rotates the space. Every component is a mix of all the original features,
   so an eigenvalue alone says nothing about one original feature's importance.

BOX-COX RECIPE
==============

1. PURPOSE: Stabilize variance (fix heteroscedasticity)

2. FORMULA: T(y) = (y^λ - 1) / λ

3. SPECIAL CASES:
   λ = 1  → no transform     λ = 0   → log(y)
   λ = 0.5 → √y              λ = -1  → 1/y

4. HOW: R finds optimal λ automatically (boxcox function)

5. WHEN: Residual plot shows funnel shape (variance not constant)

DETRENDING
==========
Remove time trend before analyzing relationships:
  y_detrended = y - (a₀ + a₁ × time)
Prevents spurious correlations caused by shared time trends.
```

## Check yourself {.reference}

Before moving on, try to answer these without scrolling up:

1. What problem does PCA solve? When would you use it?
2. What is an eigenvector in PCA terms? What does the eigenvalue tell you?
3. Why must you standardize before PCA?
4. You run PCA and keep only PC1 and PC2 (85% variance). A colleague says
   you're losing important information. Could they be right? Why?
5. What does Box-Cox fix? How do you detect the problem it solves?
6. $\lambda = 0$ in Box-Cox means you should apply which transformation?
7. You find a strong correlation between umbrella sales and car accidents.
   What should you do before concluding umbrellas cause accidents?
8. PCA gives you 5 components from 20 features. How do you decide which
   components to keep?
9. The first eigenvalue is much larger than the rest. Can you conclude that
   the first original covariate is the most important one? Why not?
